units: two neighboring workshops run on opposite principles
the joiner takes material away with his cutting tool
the wood lifts off as a curled ribbon
the smith reshapes the heated metal without losing any of it
the bar changes shape under the blows
both craftsmen show the same kind of patience
each material warns the worker about its resistance
missing that warning ends in a broken piece
text: Stand between two workshops that share a single wall and you meet two opposite ideas of what making means. In the first, the plane rides forward and the board gives way: a thin ribbon of wood lifts, curls over, and drops to the floor, and the surface grows smoother with every pass. Matter leaves the piece and never returns. In the second, nothing leaves at all. The smith brings his hammer down on hot iron and the bar stretches, thickens, bends, yet weighs exactly what it weighed before. One workman subtracts, the other merely displaces. Still, the two of them wait alike. Every material speaks first and says where it will yield and where it will hold. Wood warns through its grain, iron through its color. Whoever misses that warning splits the piece, and the whole workshop answers him with an embarrassed hush.

units: a beginner recounts his first months in a locksmith shop
the clamping tool holds the piece without marking it
the teeth of the file clog when it is worked at a wrong angle
the shop supervisor cuts a checking template out of sheet metal
an overtightened screw snapped inside its hole
polishing before flattening forces the work to be started again
the upkeep habits include greasing the jaws
classroom theory meant nothing to him before the work of his hands
text: A first-year locksmith sorts his opening months into three sets of memories. The tools come first. The vise grips hard enough to hold a piece and gently enough to leave no mark. The file loads up with metal the moment he attacks a surface at a careless angle. The shop supervisor cuts a template out of sheet steel so that every corner can be checked against something fixed. Mistakes come next: a notch driven too deep, a screw forced until it snapped off inside its hole, a face polished before it was ever brought flat, which sent the whole job back to where it began. The habits of upkeep close the list. Clear the file with a wire card, grease the jaws, shelve the templates by family of profile. He admits that the classroom meant nothing to him until he had felt the metal push back against the blade in his own hand.

units: the piece must be held still before any work begins
the marks are scribed with a metal point
the cavity is chopped first with a chisel, in short bites
the bottom of the cavity is finished with a hollow blade
a slack fit ruins the strength of the joint
the male part is sawn outside the scribed line
a dry trial checks that the entry takes moderate pressure
glue is spread only once that trial has succeeded
text: Work on a mortise and tenon joint properly begins only once the bench is clear and the stock sits perfectly still under the holdfast. Lay the joint out first of all, scribing both parts with a steel point rather than a pencil, the gauge held flat against the edge. Chop the mortise next with a chisel, taking short bites and working from the middle outward toward each end. Pare the bottom of the housing with a gouge and leave the cheeks alone, because a slack fit robs the joint of the strength it was cut for. Only then saw the tenon, keeping the blade outside the scribed line, and bring it down to size with fine paring cuts. Bring the two parts together dry: if steady palm pressure alone seats the tenon, the fit is right. Glue follows that trial and nothing else, and the clamps go on immediately afterward.

units: the last tannery in the valley is about to stop working
the price of energy has climbed steeply
the vats of the works are worn out
the expected buyer dropped the plan for want of money
the leather workshops nearby will have to buy from far away
waiting times on supplies are going to stretch
the closing works took in two trainees a year
a cooperative takeover is being talked about locally
text: The last tannery still working in the valley is closing, and the leather workshops around it are uneasy. The chain of causes behind the decision is short. Energy bills climbed steeply, the vats reached the end of their service life, and the buyer everyone expected walked away once his funding fell through. The first effect is already plain. Shops that used to fetch their hides a few steps from their own door will order them from far off instead, waiting longer for each delivery and judging the quality of the skins at a distance. A second effect touches training. The tannery took on two apprentices every year, the only place within reach where vegetable tanning could be learned by hand. Officials in the valley speak of a cooperative buyout. The craftsmen fear the order book will fold before it arrives.

units: wood dust has taken over the whole workshop
it works its way into the joints of the machines
it sets the man at the saw coughing
opening the windows only walks the cloud around
every machine has been hooked up to a soft hose
a collector box has been set up outside
a cloth filter holds back the finest particles
the dust that is caught goes into a neighbor's animal bedding
text: Push the workshop door open and you spot the trouble straight off: sawdust. It coats the floor, settles along the beams, creeps into the hinges of every machine, and has had the fellow at the saw coughing since the beginning of the week. The windows stay wide open, but the draft only walks the gray cloud from one end of the room to the other. What the joiner finally came up with is nothing clever. He ran a soft hose from each machine out to a collector box parked under a tin roof behind the wall. A cloth sleeve holds the finest stuff back, and a sack underneath takes the rest. He still sweeps, of course, but he no longer breathes his own shop. And the dust, instead of going on the fire, goes down the road to a neighbor who spreads it as bedding for his animals. The air, he swears, smells of cut wood again.

units: the writer weighs learning at a screen against learning at a bench
a filmed movement can be stopped and pulled apart
teaching in a classroom wastes no material
the workshop costs money and wears the machines down
every failed attempt turns wood into scrap
only the workshop passes on what the tool feels like
an aching forearm tells the learner the pressure is wrong
the writer holds that what the classroom saves will be paid back later
text: Should a trade be learned at a screen or at a bench? Training centers are split on the question, and the comparison deserves an honest, unflattering hearing. The classroom has a real edge. A filmed movement can be halted, run again, pulled apart step by step, and a poor posture corrected without spoiling a single board. The workshop, for its part, eats money, wears the machines down, and turns wood into scrap every time a beginner misses. What it gives back is what no screen will ever hand over: the tool trembling in the palm, the smell of glue that is setting badly, the ache in the forearm that says the pressure is wrong. Drop that side of the training and you turn out graduates who can describe a joint they would never manage to cut. The arithmetic is false. The bench collects later what the classroom kept.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the villagers name her by her trade and nothing else
her hands carry old scars
she no longer tells where those cuts came from
her tools are ranked by width on her bench
the handle of her mallet has been worn smooth by use
a grinding wheel brings the edges back
she holds that a block is chosen before it is shaped
she will not show unfinished work to anyone
some ten pupils have come through her shop
she started as a laborer before a cutting tool was put in her hand
text: In the village she is the stonecutter, and the word does for a name. Her hands come first: broad, dry, crossed with old cuts whose stories she has long since stopped telling. Then her tools, laid out on the bench with something close to tenderness, the mallet worn smooth at the grip, the chisels ranked by width, the wheel that brings each edge back and fills the shed with a bright hiss. Then her road into the trade: she came in as a laborer and pushed a barrow for a whole year before anyone put a chisel in her hand. Then her rules: a block is chosen before it is cut, a flaw is worked around rather than hidden, and unfinished work is shown to nobody. Some ten pupils have come through her shop, three of them still cutting stone in the valley. They will carve truly, she says, once they stop counting their blows.

units: a panel judges a chest in the order it was built
the timber that was chosen shows an even color
the joint marks were not carried over from one template
a gap shows up at the corner set at the back
the cuts that were made run true and close tight
the finishing stage lets the judges down
abrasive marks remain beside the metal fittings
the wax went onto a surface that still carried dust
the piece is called sturdy despite a rushed last stage
text: The chest presented to the panel is best judged in the order it was built. The timber comes off well: cut through the quarter, quiet grain, an even color running from board to board. The layout that follows already wavers, because the dovetail marks were never carried over from one master template, and the drift shows at the corner at the back. The execution wins a good part of that ground back. The saw cuts run true, the sockets are clean, and the joints close tight without being forced. The finishing stage is where the work slips. Sanding was rushed, grinder marks still catch the light beside the hinges, and wax laid over a surface that had not been wiped has frozen a haze of fine scratches into the wood. What the panel will finally remember is a sturdy piece whose last hour gave the maker away.

units: the craftsman announces a delay of two weeks on an order
the wood he had planned on was soaked under a torn cover
its moisture runs higher than his shop will accept
using that wood would shrink the panels once they were assembled
the drawers would bind as soon as the heating season came
the boards have been stacked in the drying kiln
the work starts again on an older batch
the new shade is darker than was foreseen
photographs will be sent at the dry assembly
text: I am writing about the chest of drawers you entrusted to me, which will now reach you two weeks later than agreed. The wood itself is the reason. The batch I had set aside spent a long spell under a canvas cover that had split open, and it carries far more moisture than my shop will accept. Worked as it stands, the panels would shrink once assembled, and the drawers would bind as soon as the heating season came round. I have stacked those boards in the drying kiln, then, and started again from an older batch, which pushes the whole job further back. One agreeable thing comes out of the delay: the older wood runs to a deeper shade, and I will suggest a pale wax that brings it forward. I will send photographs as soon as the piece stands dry, so you can settle the choice before any glue is spread.

units: a restorer is blamed for how slowly she prices a job
every piece of furniture hides repairs made earlier
an assessment made too fast leads to costs nobody saw coming
she takes part of the object apart before naming a price
this inspection is charged to the owner
half of her clients refuse to pay for it
she now offers a pair of estimates
the survey fee is credited back if the work is hers to do
quarrels with clients have almost stopped
text: What does a furniture restorer say when clients grumble that her pricing takes too long? She names the problem plainly: every piece hides a history of earlier repairs, and a rushed reading of it ends in bills nobody saw coming. Asked how she goes about the job, she describes taking part of the piece apart, testing the glue joints, looking behind the backboards, and only then naming a price she means to hold. Asked what that care costs, she grants that she charges for it and that one owner in two turns it down. Her answer is a pair of estimates: a survey fee, credited back if the restoration is hers to do, and a wide figure for anyone who wants an answer on the spot. Quarrels have almost stopped since. One difficulty stays, which is persuading a hurried owner that patience costs less than doing the work twice.
